executive_assessment.text: Beryl impacts differed sharply among Union Island, Mayreau, Canouan, Bequia and Mustique, with named water, health and transport damage.
Five named schools and Union Island/Mayreau training add concrete recovery inputs; policy proposals and fabrication applications remain plans or reported outputs.

geographic_notes.text: Source dated 2024-07-26 reports: Beryl brought Category 3–4 winds to the Southern Grenadines; building damage was extreme on Union Island, extremely severe on Mayreau, severe on Canouan and much lower on Bequia and Mustique.

Source dated 2024-07-26 reports: On Union Island, Beryl damaged the hospital, water network, power plant, airport and nearly all berthing structures; on Palm Island it damaged a desalination plant, while Mayreau suffered major structural and communications damage.

Source dated 2019-08-02 reports: The 2019 policy identifies low-lying Grenadines coralline islets as exposed to sea-level rise and storm surge, with coral-bleaching risk to Tobago Cays; lower rainfall also contributes to drought and saltwater-intrusion pressure.

Source dated 2026-03-27 reports: UNDP reports a two-day disaster-management and school-safety workshop at the Tobago Cays Marine Park office for teachers and disaster-committee members from Union Island and Mayreau.

Source dated 2026-03-27 reports: The programme reports EC$385,000 of equipment supplied to Paget Farm Primary, Mayreau Primary, Union Island Secondary, Stephanie Browne Primary and Mary Hutchinson Primary.

Source dated 2025-12-16 reports: UNDP reports that 20 Union Island students, educators, community members and entrepreneurs took part in hands-on design and fabrication training; a 3D printer was handed to Union Island Secondary School.

Source dated 2025-12-16 reports: UNDP says Beryl-related isolation and disrupted supply chains can delay imported parts; the workshop presented local fabrication of water-pipe connectors and fishing-gear parts as possible emergency uses.

known_gaps.text: Automated machine-screening is not independent source verification or human approval. 16 of 17 evidence records and 0 of 0 pathways lack claim-level verification in this remediation; review the linked records before relying on them.
No countrywide causal estimate of climate impacts on conflict or violence is established by these sources.
Full subnational coverage and independently evaluated long-term response effectiveness remain gaps.

National and selected local examples do not establish district-level coverage or causal attribution.
The bank contains no completed mediated climate-FCV pathway; this is an evidence gap, not evidence of absence.
Beryl evacuation and service disruption do not establish violent conflict or event attribution.
No inspected source establishes a climate-conflict or violence-to-adaptation pathway in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines; none is inferred.
The GRADE report is a rapid July 2024 estimate; approximately 600 damaged buildings on Saint Vincent were not disaggregated locally, and some island damage data were preliminary.
The government climate-policy vulnerability evidence dates mainly through 2019; its proposed adaptation measures are not implementation results.
UNDP reports local training and handovers but provides no independent evaluation of response performance or resilience outcomes.
The UNDP Water for Resilience and Union Island small-grants project pages could not be read directly; no search-indexed findings were used.
A World Bank project appraisal document was excluded from findings because it is marked FOR OFFICIAL USE ONLY, despite public hosting.
No climate–violence pathway is inferred from hazard exposure or recovery gaps; local infrastructure and capacity evidence stands on its own.
